newsitem.title: CHINA: China theatregoers see elderly Deng for first time.
newsitem.headline: China theatregoers see elderly Deng for first time.

text.p: The audience gasped, then cheered, as they saw for the first time the man who transformed China from sluggish Stalinist backwater into economic powerhouse portrayed on stage as a national leader.
Before his death at the age of 92 last February, Deng Xiaoping could never be depicted in theatre or film in any other role than that of youthful soldier-strategist.

Deng's first stage portrayal, in the play "Return!", is part of an orgy of celebration across China for the handover of Hong Kong at midnight on Monday, a resumption of sovereignty made possible by Deng's own "one country, two systems" formula.

"This is a great moment for me," said actor Pan Yumin, his resemblance striking as he waited in full make-up to go on stage for the premiere on Saturday, dressed in Deng's trademark grey Mao suit, his feet tucked into the traditional black cloth shoes Deng preferred.

"This is the first time that this great leader has been portrayed at any stage of his life after the Liberation," Pan said, referring to the 1949 communist takeover. "I can't claim to be any part of history... but I must do my best."
The tradition not to allow mere mortals to portray a top leader until his entry to the communist pantheon in the skies was set both with Chairman Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai.

Films abound in which actors depict a young, vigorous Deng defeating the Japanese in World War Two or triumphant over the Nationalists in the civil war that ended in 1949. It was regarded as disrespectful to portray the leader as an old man -- he did not take power until he was 74.

On stage in "Return!", Deng occupies the stage for a brief three-minute adaptation of his 1982 meeting with British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher that led to the negotiations that sealed the return of Hong Kong after 156 years of British colonial rule.

Deng dominates the final scene, a moment of sheer socialist hyperbole as he waves to the audience against a backdrop showing Hong Kong's skyline while dozens of smiling children dressed in communist red and waving flowers cluster around him shouting "Grandpa Deng".
"It's propaganda," Polish actress Basha Weiss who plays Thatcher said of the play. "I'm having a little problem with that... I do it. I'm an actress."
The Shanghai-born Pan has spent the three years since he was discovered as the lookalike who would play Deng after his death, practising to imitate Deng's broad Sichuan accent.
"Other people wake up and switch on the radio, I wake up and switch on my tape recorder to listen to Deng Xiaoping," Pan said in an interview.
For Pan, 60, this could be the role of his career.

"I am too short, so I was never able to play leading roles," he said. For Deng, who was just 150 cm (4ft 11 inches) tall, Pan is just right and expects to play him in a film of his years as China's most powerful man that is in the planning stages.
"I hope I will be able to portray Deng for many years. I have two goals in life, one to play Deng Xiaoping and second to prepare myself to play Deng Xiaoping."

Pan has had to make a few cosmetic changes to perfect the Deng look. Deng's hair was thinner, his eyebrows bushier and his neck shorter, plus Deng was slightly pigeon-toed and Pan said he walks more like a duck with his toes turned out.

"Deng Xiaoping did not have any really distinguishing traits in the way he moved or spoke, so that makes it quite difficult to play him," Pan said. "What I have done is to read all his works, his speeches so that I can understand his personality."
